title: SPECIAL REPORT: Kotek v. Drazan, It’s a Longtime Rivalry Seeking New Audiences - The Corvallis Advocate
content: In her second quest to defeat Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, Sen. Christine Drazan, R-Canby, has gone straight into the political lion’s den. She has announced policy plans to reduce taxes and regulations in the heavily-Democratic Portland metropolitan area, emphasized the natural beauty of its waterfront and advocated against needle exchanges near schools in Multnomah County. But those appeals haven’t always gone smoothly. At one speaking event in Portland, attendees peppered her with questions about her relationship with the national GOP. During a September meeting at a Southeast Portland church, one voter accused Drazan of misrepresenting her life story about politicians failing a timber industry that left her Klamath Falls hometown. Despite the effective rematch from 2022, this year’s gubernatorial campaign trail has pushed both Drazan and Kotek to appeal to the opposite side of their ideological lanes. Polling a few weeks out from the Nov. 3 election showed the race in a statistical tie, and the two women’s rhetorical skills are being tested in ways that their allies say are naturally uncomfortable for the candidates. Drazan’s has been campaigning in person while supporting downballot Republicans and focusing on metropolitan areas. She no longer has to fortify support in rural areas where she may have lost votes to nonaffiliated challenger Betsy Johnson in the 2022 race, but that has opened her up to at times hostile interactions from skeptical voters in the state’s most populous county. “Is it easy? Absolutely not. Is it comfortable to go into those settings as a Republican? Absolutely not,” said former Republican Rep. Knute Buehler, a Drazan ally who lost to former Gov. Kate Brown in the 2018 election and has since left the Republican party. “But it’s absolutely essential to do.” Kotek also faces significant headwinds. She is seeking to appease business-friendly voters in suburban and urban areas of the state while motivating a fractured progressive base in Portland. Many of her appearances have focused on interviews with sympathetic social media influencers rather than campaign press conferences or public events. Ahead of her first term, Kotek named housing and homelessness, behavioral health and education as her top three priorities. But during her nearly four years in office, Oregon has struggled to make progress on each of those issues. Tens of millions in new state funding netted thousands of new shelter beds and kept tens of thousands of Oregonians from eviction, but the most recent federal count of homeless individuals found thousands more people lacked homes in 2025 than in 2023. Oregon students’ grasp of reading, writing, math and science has improved slightly since immediate post-pandemic lows, but they’re still far behind their peers. The governor has spent most of the campaign trying to tie Drazan to the Trump administration and began to deviate from that messaging in her final two debates earlier this month. Her supporters say the task of showing progress is not within her natural skillset. “She’s an in-the-weeds person, and she’s a big picture person, and she is terrible at taking credit for it,” said former Portland Democratic Rep. Barbara Smith Warner, who was House majority leader when Kotek was House speaker. “You can get plenty of stuff done if you don’t take credit, and yet there’s a point where it is different when you’re a leader.” Kotek first came onto Oregon’s political scene as an advocate for the Oregon Food Bank in the late 1990s after moving from Pennsylvania, eventually winning election to a Portland-area House seat in 2006. She later became the state’s longest-serving House speaker from 2013 to 2022 and shepherded major progressive policies, such as the nation’s strongest set of sanctuary protections for immigrants and a universal paid leave program, through the Legislature. She’s one of the nation’s first two openly lesbian governors. She’s also among the least popular governors in the nation, polling has shown throughout her term. In an interview, Kotek conveyed a sense of urgency for building on her work, such as getting Oregon to buck a national trend to increase initial housing starts for 2026. The estimated nearly 9,700 home permits pulled so far this year still puts Oregon far below her initial goal of 36,000 new homes per year to address decades of underbuilding. “I’ve never said that the mission is accomplished, but what I have said is we have to keep working together to make progress,” she said. “Progress takes persistence, that takes leadership and continuity.” But that continuity has also been marked with some scrutiny over the role some of Kotek’s closest allies, including first lady Aimee Kotek Wilson and labor union leaders, have played in the Oregon government. Several of Kotek’s top advisers left her office over her 2024 attempt to elevate her wife’s authority by creating an “Office of the First Spouse” and giving Kotek Wilson, who has a background in social work, a role in crafting behavioral health policy. The Oregon Government Ethics Commission dismissed complaints against Kotek on the grounds that there was no evidence that Kotek or her wife would benefit from an unpaid volunteer position. The governor has since tapped the first lady to lead a council aiming to address workforce issues for behavioral health services in Oregon. When it comes to unions, meanwhile, Kotek has faced backlash for their influence on a variety of issues, such as unemployment benefits, public projects and legislative districting. Her support for a 2025 first-in-the-nation law offering unemployment benefits to striking public and private workers, for instance, reignited longstanding concerns that she wasn’t serving as an effective check on their interests. Critics see the law as a giveaway to unions that will strain public agencies and the state’s unemployment insurance fund. Kotek also issued a 2024 executive order that required many state construction projects to be built with union labor, a type of proposal which industry groups have long criticized for driving up costs. After a coalition of organizations led by the Oregon-Columbia chapter of the Associated General Contractors sued, a Marion County judge blocked the order in March. Unions were also thorn in the side for some in Kotek’s party during a special 2021 legislative session near the end of her tenure as House speaker, when state lawmakers sought to redraw legislative and congressional maps. Former Rep. Marty Wilde, D-Eugene, said he saw the hand of influential unions who support Democrats in the decision to redraw his Eugene-area district into one favoring Republicans and box him out of the Senate seat he was considering seeking. The Oregonian/OregonLive reported that the executive director of the state’s largest public employee union had been advising House Democrats during the session. “I never felt like it was personal on Tina’s part, but pretty clearly the public employee unions had given marching orders, and the Senate had a certain outcome that they wanted,” Wilde said. “When I objected to that, I became political roadkill.” The governor has maintained on the campaign trail that donors and unions do not determine her decisions. While political action committees affiliated with the Service Employees International Union have given her more than $1 million so far this campaign, the Oregon Education Association that represents roughly 41,000 teachers has pointedly declined to endorse her. Political jockeying aside, Kotek allies say her strength remains in policy details. The governor notes that she has replaced many agency directors since taking office, and that her agencies have complied with several audits. Her plan for a second term focuses on improving affordability through more housing resources for renters and first-time buyers and more social services such as a universal state-funded preschool program, though how to pay for it remains an open question. “I’m a very deliberate person,” Kotek said. “We have put some experts together. They’re coming up with a plan to look at what we have, look where we need to go, look at how we can get there in the next three to four years. That is, I think, a signature piece of a second term for me.” Next January will mark 40 years since Oregon’s last Republican governor, Vic Atiyeh, left office. During his two campaigns, Atiyeh managed to capitalize on his ties to business communities to spur economic development. That’s the brand of politics Drazan describes to Portland voters at a home featured in a September campaign video. Drazan, the former House Republican leader who butted heads with Kotek in 2020 and 2021, said national politics has its “own weather system that I have never been drug into.” Drazan’s campaign did not respond to multiple interview requests over four weeks. The senator grew up in Klamath Falls and often talks about her family struggling to make ends meet and relying on food stamps after her father lost his mill job. She served as House minority leader from 2019 to 2021, and she resigned to run for her first gubernatorial bid the next year. She returned to Salem in 2025 and served as House minority leader again, joining the Senate in October last year to fill the seat of former Sen. Daniel Bonham, a Republican from The Dalles who left to work for the Trump administration. She originally entered politics in the 1990s as a legislative aide and climbed the ranks to a chief of staff position with then-Oregon House Speaker Mark Simmons. Drazan became accustomed to a Republican Legislature working to earn the signature of a Democratic governor, an arrangement she argues can be replicated in reverse with her governorship. But something changed, Drazan and her allies say, when she returned to Salem in 2019 as a freshman House lawmaker in the minority. She recounts for voters a committee chair telling her that she killed her anti-bullying bill that year “because I could,” an example of partisanship that left her feeling discontent with engaging in good-faith across party lines. Smith Warner, the chair of the committee where Drazan’s bill died, disputed Drazan’s account: “While it sounds like something I would say, it doesn’t sound like an answer I would give about that specifically.” Lawmakers went on to pass similar legislation two years later following advocacy from the parents of a child who committed suicide, which Drazan describes as too little, too late. Her 2019 bill, which sought to notify parents when a child experiences harassment or bullying in an Oregon school, died in the Committee on Student Success without a vote. “I ran to be a Republican leader right after that session,” Drazan said. “Not because I am a partisan, but because I felt so shocked and offended by the power systems that I was operating in that I wanted more balance.” Drazan is already making an effort to show that she can work across the aisle, touting the governor’s prosperity council’s findings from earlier this year as a starting point for legislative conversations in 2027. Two of Drazan’s priorities are changing the estate tax, which taxes dead people’s assets beginning at $1 million, and the corporate activity tax on businesses for more than $1 million in commercial activity, taxes that the council identified as areas of potential change. “Do you know how to play the game? Can you negotiate with the majority party? Can you do all those sorts of things?” asked Bryan Iverson, a Republican political consultant and husband of Rep. Vikki Breese-Iverson, R-Prineville. “I think Drazan has always been adept at both of those.” Her actions in practice, however, have sometimes aligned with the more polarizing cultural and social priorities of the right. She has sponsored bills to overturn mail-in voting, bar transgender youth from sports in alignment with their gender identity and create criminal liability for abortion providers. She issued a statement decrying “domestic terrorists” and calling for “order” after Trump threatened to deploy the National Guard to Portland last year, though she has denied that her statement welcomed federal troops to Oregon. At the same time, Drazan has said she is a supporter of Oregon’s status as the first-in-the-nation sanctuary state for immigrants and will respect Oregon’s abortion law. She has spoken out against the Trump administration’s tariffs and the war with Iran. She often says she is a person of faith who has her own standards she does not seek to impose upon others. “This is our place and I will serve the people of this state,” Drazan said in Portland’s Lents neighborhood, “no matter who’s in the White House, no matter who’s in majority control of the Legislature or anywhere else.” By Shaanth Kodialam Nanguneri of news partner Oregon Capital Chronicle Do you have a story for The Advocate? title: Honda’s All-New 2028 CR-V Is Coming by Spring 2027, and It May Go Hybrid-Only Like the RAV4 - Torque News
content: The 2028 Honda CR-V is on the way, scheduled for a spring 2027 launch, and we’re learning more and more. We still don’t know everything - for example, it’s unclear if the next Honda CR-V will be hybrid only or, as with today’s CR-V, offer both an internal-combustion engine option or a hybrid powertrain. Let’s take a look at the newest reporting on the subject. It’s pretty clear, based on the reporting from various outlets, that the 2028 Honda CR-V will be a full redesign, not just a refresh. The difference is this - redesigns are often a complete re-do of the vehicle, sometimes including the frame and powertrain, whereas refreshes tend to involve mild styling changes (inside and out) and either few mechanical changes or none. Sometimes a redesign splits the difference - the frame and other mechanical bits under the skin don’t change too much, but the exterior and interior look completely different. That does muddy the waters a bit in terms of a definition, but in this case, it seems Honda is aiming for a full redesign. The biggest question is this - will the next CR-V be hybrid only, or simply offer that as an option? We’ve reported extensively on how the next Honda Ridgeline might be hybrid only. That truck uses a larger V6 while the gas CR-V has a 1.5-liter turbocharged four, and it’s obviously on a different platform, so there’s no direct correlation. However, if Honda is serious about increasing electrification of its fleet, especially in a time of sky-high gas prices, it might go hybrid-only with many of its models, perhaps all save the sports cars. After all, the strategy seems to be working well for Toyota. The current hybrid combines a 2.0-liter four-cylinder gas engine with an electric motor. Circling back to exterior styling, Cars Direct reports that changes to the exterior could include new front- and rear-end designs, new wheels, new lights, and new paint colors. Inside, expect a new dashboard design, new controls, nicer materials, and new trim. This author hopes Honda finally upgrades its outdated infotainment system as part of the change. Vehicles almost always get bigger when redesigned. If that happens here, there should be more interior space. We’d expect to see the next CR-V go on sale next spring, based on the reporting from Cars Direct. That means it could be shown at the 2026 Los Angeles Auto Show this fall or the 2027 North American International Auto Show in Detroit, which takes place in January. It’s unclear where it will be built. Current models are built in Indiana, Ohio, and Canada. Tariffs could affect that decision. Toyota just launched its newest RAV4, the CR-V’s biggest rival, this year. Jeep also launched its newest Cherokee, which plays in that segment, in 2026. The next Ford Bronco Sport is likely on its way. Subaru has been overhauling its lineup and has redesigned and refreshed models ready to take on the CR-V. Honda’s CR-V is popular, but with a new Toyota RAV4 already out, the company will have to play catchup in the crowded and competitive segment. As noted above, if the CR-V moves to a hybrid-only powertrain, that would be a big step forward for Honda, which has indicated in the past that it wants to make its vehicle fleet more electrified. Electrification as a strategy generally means a mix of hybrids (including plug-ins) and battery-electric vehicles. Going hybrid only also allows the company to match Toyota. On the other hand, offering a gas engine could appeal to the hybrid hesitant - those few consumers who might be concerned about the cost of a hybrid, be it upfront or in terms of maintenance and repair over time. We’ll see what happens - we could know all about the next CR-V as soon as next month. If not then, then soon enough, especially if the spring of 2027 is a launch target. title: How we got here: Summary of U.S. v. Valerie Hayes, the ‘Mennonite kidnapping’ case - Augusta Free Press
content: In the late hours of July 29, 2018, a young Old Order Mennonite couple were getting ready for bed. The government says that’s when a long, drawn-out plan to kidnap five Old Order children from two respective families and execute their parents came to end. Alleged ringleader Valerie Hayes and two of her three co-conspirators came close but failed to get the couple’s 8-month-old and 2-year-old into their getaway vehicle before killing their parents and going to the second home, but that’s just the tip of the iceberg. “Although the facts of this case read like the script of a bad horror movie, the defendants’ murderous plot was real and it posed a grave risk to their intended victims,” U.S. Attorney Thomas Cullen said in a 2019 news release. The cast of characters includes Valerie Hayes and married couple Frank and Jennifer Frank Amnott, and Hayes’ boyfriend, Gary Blake Reburn, who didn’t make his entrance until the day before the failed attempt. At the heart of the plot were Hayes and the Amnotts, who met through a mutual friend in 2014. The Florida couple wanted to have children, but Jennifer’s pregnancies all ended in miscarriage. The government says that for several years, Hayes had told “people in her orbit” that she was a secret agent who went on dangerous missions through which she could arrange the adoption of abused or neglected children. Hayes and the Amnotts become close. The Amnotts had spent most of their lives in their home state of Florida, with a brief period in Texas. Hayes lived with the two on different occasions within both states, with the Amnotts occasionally visiting Hayes in her Maryland home where she lived with her boyfriend, Gary Blake Reburn. Between their introduction and the failed kidnapping and murder plot four years later, Hayes told the couple that she had located a child for them to adopt twice. In or about the fall of 2016, she said she had secured the first child. During the Christmas season, the couple took to social media to announce that a child would be entering their lives in the coming year. In February, the couple were told that instead of obtaining the baby from a third party that Hayes herself was carrying the child. In March, the couple learned by way of a text from a supposed “colleague” that Hayes had been attacked, suffering multiple stab wounds in the belly that killed the baby. Then, in July 2017, Hayes allegedly told the Amnotts that she had secured another baby-to-be but that child also failed to arrive. It was after that alleged ruse that Hayes is accused of telling the couple that three of her own children – Ronan, Zippy and Leona—had been captured and were in the possession of two Old Order Mennonite families in Dayton, and she needed to take them back. Hayes said two other children had to be taken, as well, one of which they could adopt. The couple agreed to join her mission. Both have entered guilty pleas and will testify during the February trial. Days before the failed attempt, the Amnotts headed for Hayes’ Kensington, Maryland home, where Jennifer would watch Hayes’ three biological daughters while her husband, Frank, and went to Dayton. Frank Amnott has told investigators that there were four or five child safety seats in a silver Mercedes “van.” The government says that on July 27, a Friday, the two spent the day surveilling the homes that Hayes had chosen. The first, where the effort came to a halt, was located a stone’s throw from a county road intersection within sight of a key location. The second was located several miles away. The plan was to wait for the fathers to milk their cows the following morning. At the first house, they would wait until the father had gone into the milking parlor, after which they would go inside the house, where one would restrain the mother while the other secured the couple’s children. One of them would then take the mother to the nearby woods and execute her with a shot to the head. The two would then go into the barn or wait for the father to return to the house and execute him, as well. Frank Amnott told investigators that both he and Hayes were armed as they waited outside the house as planned. But then what appeared to be a “helping hand” showed up to help the father with the milking. With the plan at a dead end, Hayes decided it was time to go home and ask her boyfriend to be “an extra set of hands and eyes.” Reburn agreed. Along the two-hour return, Hayes changed into a cape dress and a covering to appear as an Old Order Mennonite. Documents don’t say where or when Hayes obtained her disguise, but the reason was no mystery: Hayes wanted to appear as a member of the community, which she felt may work to their advantage. When Sunday morning again included two men milking the cows, the group came up with plan B: make off with the children while the couple was getting ready for bed. Throughout all of this, Jennifer Amnott stayed in touch with the group through texts. But, as seen through the eyes of the Amnotts and Reburn, they weren’t alone. The government says beginning the morning of Sunday, July 29, Hayes was surreptitiously using texts from two purported security personnel. She had long spoken of associates who served to protect her safety. “Bjorn” oversaw the fake two-man operation, which included surveillance both on the ground and in the air by way of drones. That to leave her co-conspirators assured that all was clear. Having gained confidence, Frank Amnott and Reburn joined Hayes in an alleged search of the first house while the family was at church. While inside, they observed the layout of the house and the size of the children’s clothing, among other things. Approaching dark, the group asked the bogus “intel” operatives for guidance. Convinced that the time was right, the three were ready to strike. According to court documents, Hayes and Frank Amnott dropped Reburn off by the house to wait until the light went off. The two then approached the house in their vehicle and turned off the headlights. After getting out of the vehicle, they met Reburn at the front of the house. While they were en route, the father turned on the lights and opened the door. When he saw that they were armed, he tried to close it but outnumbered three to one, he wasn’t able. Frank Amnott and Reburn took the father to the basement, where he was laid on the ground face down with his wrists zip-tied behind his back, and asked where his wife was. The father said he didn’t know at which time Amnott held the father at gunpoint and Reburn headed upstairs, where he heard Hayes calling out for the mother, whose name she had learned when the three were inside the house earlier. By that time, it was too late. Having seen the three break in, the mother grabbed the couple’s cordless phone and ran into the cornfield across the road, where she called police. When a deputy that was close by arrived, he saw the mother standing in front of the house with Hayes and Reburn. The mother stood frozen and said nothing, fearing Hayes and Reburn would shoot the deputy if she spoke. Believing them to be neighbors or bystanders, the deputy directed them to drop the mother off for her safety at the one-pump convenience store a stone’s throw away. The deputy then went into the house, where he found the children safe upstairs. His search ended when he found Frank Amnott in the basement with his gun pointed at the father. Amnott then put down the gun, put up his hands and was arrested without incident. It was during the deputy’s search that Hayes and Amnott dropped off the mother and the corner store and left for Hayes and Reburns’ home, where they met Frank Amnott’s wife, Jennifer, who had learned by text that her husband had been left behind. When Hayes’ oldest daughter told the three that she had seen Frank Amnott’s arrest on the news, they immediately sprang into action and left for Scotland, where they were arrested four months later. After a 7-year battle to avoid extradition, the European Court of Human Rights refused to hear their case. The three were then sent back to the U.S., where they were arraigned in Charlottesville federal court, with all three taken to the Albemarle-Charlottesville Regional Jail. Hayes and Jennifer Amnot were arraigned last Oct. 28, with Reburn arraigned the following day. A series of hearings have been held since their arraignment one year ago. The next will be held on Tuesday. The case’s twists and turns leave many questions to be answered during the February trial, which is expected to last all month. One thing that is missing from its 158 documents is the fact that Valerie Hayes herself was a member of the Mennonite church during her teens. Then Valerie Perfect, she was 14 when her family joined a conservative Mennonite congregation in the area where the failed kidnapping and murder conspiracy took place. The church was not Old Order, but living and worshipping in the heart of Old Order country gave her an understanding of both its landscape and the lifestyle of Old Order Mennonites. The government has not described the couple that was targeted as Old Order Mennonites. Instead, the case is referred to as the “Mennonite kidnapping.”  Should the case and expected trial make national headlines, it could be frustrating for the thousands of Mennonites who live in greater Harrisonburg, a Mennonite mecca filled with scores of Mennonite churches that are predominately mainstream. Wake Forest and Virginia reportedly had an agreement in the summer to go black (Wake) and orange (Virginia) with their uniform color schemes for their scheduled Saturday, Oct. 31 game. title: State of Florida v. Jermaine Mandell Williams Sr. - 7th Judicial Circuit State Attorney's Office
content: Judge Sentences Williams to Death for Brutal Murder of His Wife BUNNELL – Defendant Jermaine Williams Sr. was sentenced to death during a hearing on Monday. In July, a Flagler County jury voted 11-1 in favor of the death penalty for Williams for the First-Degree Murder of his wife. On Aug. 2, 2024, Williams stabbed his wife in the street outside of their Bunnell home. The victim’s 14-year-old son witnessed the stabbing and tried to intervene. The defendant’s father, who lives nearby, happened upon the scene and held Williams at gunpoint until he stepped away from the victim. The victim was stabbed 19-20 times. She was taken to the hospital, where she died from her injuries. Surveillance video captured the defendant going inside the home and returning with an eight-inch chef’s knife before attacking the victim. After his arrest, Williams admitted he retrieved the knife from the kitchen and stabbed his wife multiple times. He told detectives a comment she made “pushed him over the edge.” “The video footage shows a chilling and merciless killing. The defendant stabbed his wife 20 times while their 14-year-old son watched,” State Attorney R.J. Larizza said about the case. “Only the defendant’s father – armed with a gun – was able to stop the brutal attack. There can be no quarter, no sympathy and no doubt that the death penalty was the only choice in this case.” Chief of Homicide Jason Lewis and Assistant State Attorney Helen Schwartz successfully argued for the death penalty for the state. The Honorable Dawn Nichols heard the case and imposed sentence. Haley Harrison | Public Information Officer | Office of State Attorney R.J. title: NFL today: How to watch Cowboys v Eagles, TV channels & live stream Monday 26 October - The Guardian
content: How will Dallas and Philadelphia fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options There is “reeling”, and then there is whatever the Eagles are doing heading into Monday Night Football against the Cowboys. Philadelphia have lost four games in a row to fall within a whisker of last place in the NFC East. Jalen Hurts’s blood clots rapidly escalated and have probably knocked the franchise QB out for the season. Backup Tanner McKee has inherited a legitimate crisis. And it’s not as if all was hunky-dory before Hurts went out. The Eagles had already blown a 10-point fourth-quarter lead to the Rams and let the Jaguars come back on them in shocking fashion in London before the Hurts news. The Cowboys have their own enormous issues. Former Eagles assistant Christian Parker joined up as defensive coordinator, aiming to fix a bad unit, but the Cowboys are still struggling to keep teams from racking up big point and yardage totals. Facing the Cowboys defense has been a salve for struggling offenses, as when a Packers team who couldn’t convert a third down for their life suddenly converted nine of their first 10 against Big D last weekend. Despite these issues, both teams are within reach of the first-place Giants in the East. This is a critical game even though it is mainly compelling for the anxieties on both sides of the rivalry. Stadium: Lincoln Financial Field (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania) United States: Watch on ESPN or ABC, or stream through Fubo or ESPN Unlimited. Fubo’s ABC availability depends on location. Canada: Stream on Fubo Sports Pro or DAZN. Fubo Sports Pro includes NFL Game Pass on DAZN. United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Main Event, or stream with NOW or NFL Game Pass on DAZN. For Philly, McKee’s comfort level will be the most important thing. In his first 2026 outing, last week’s 25-14 loss to the Panthers, McKee threw 45 passes and prioritized getting the ball out quickly to leave less time for bad things to happen. McKee averaged 3.1 completed air yards per attempt, which ranks 40th in the NFL so far this season, according to Pro Football Reference. (The idea there: McKee did not successfully complete many passes more than a few yards beyond the line of scrimmage.) Most troublingly, the Eagles got just 2.9 yards after the catch per completion, a comically low rate that would have McKee last among regular starters. The Cowboys will be on high alert for blitzes from Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, who has surely observed Dak Prescott’s trouble against the blitz over his past two games. Fangio is one of the least-blitzy defensive coordinators in the league this season, but teams have drastically escalated their blitzing against Prescott, who has poor numbers against it (no touchdowns and a passer rating of 67 when blitzed in his last two games). Could it be that the much greener McKee is not the only QB to have an ugly time in this one?

title: This Ultra-Rare 2019 Cadillac CT6-V Is Looking For A New Home - Yahoo Autos
content: Cadillac built just 915 examples of the CT6-V for the U.S. market, and one of these rare performance sedans is now up for auction. The 2019 model is listed on Cars & Bids, giving enthusiasts a chance to own one of Cadillac's most unusual modern creations. Not to be confused with the current 6.2-liter supercharged V8 found in the CT5-V Blackwing, the CT6-V has a hand-built 4.2-liter twin-turbocharged Blackwing V8 that was developed specifically for Cadillac. Despite its impressive performance, the engine disappeared almost as quickly as it arrived, with high production costs and the CT6's cancellation cutting its career short. The CT6-V arrived in 2019, just as GM was preparing to discontinue several of its sedans. Production of the CT6 ended in 2020, and the original Blackwing V8 never found its way into another model line. The example currently for sale is finished in Crystal White Tricoat with a Jet Black interior and has covered approximately 49,800 miles. It remains largely original, with the seller reporting no notable modifications apart from tinted windows. The CT6-V's Blackwing engine produces 550 horsepower and 640 lb-ft of torque, sending power to all four wheels through a 10-speed automatic transmission. Cadillac claimed the sedan could accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in approximately 3.8 seconds. Unlike Cadillac's more familiar small-block V8s, the Blackwing was a bespoke design featuring twin-scroll turbochargers, forged connecting rods, and a forged crankshaft. A less powerful version was also offered in the CT6 Platinum, which produced 500 horsepower and 574 lb-ft of torque. The Blackwing name eventually returned on the CT4-V Blackwing and CT5-V Blackwing, although neither uses this particular engine. That makes the CT6-V an unusual piece of Cadillac performance history. This example comes equipped with 20-inch Midnight Silver wheels, Magnetic Ride Control suspension, and dual sunroofs. Inside, it features heated and ventilated front seats, heated rear seats, a rear-seat entertainment system, and a Bose Panaray sound system. Its condition isn't perfect, however. The listing mentions exterior chips and scratches, bumper scuffs, wheel curb rash, and some wear on the driver's seat bolster. The Carfax report also records minor damage incidents in 2020 and 2025, with repair documentation provided. Recent maintenance includes fluid changes in October 2025 and replacement tires fitted earlier that year. At the time of writing, bidding had reached $27,750 with 12 bids placed. The Cars & Bids auction is scheduled to end on October 29, 2026. The seller also lists an Ally Premier Protection plan valid until March 2029 or 87,829 miles, subject to its terms. With bidding already underway, we'll soon find out how much buyers are willing to pay for one of Cadillac's rarest modern performance sedans. title: Director James McTeigue on How the V for Vendetta Mask Became a Global Symbol of Protest - Consequence of Sound

For the film's 20th anniversary, the filmmaker looks back on how the Guy Fawkes mask has permeated pop culture and resistance movements alike V for Vendetta director James McTeigue thinks it’s “amazing,” the way that the Guy Fawkes mask from his 2006 movie has taken on a life of its own. “When you make a film, you hope that it might seep into the culture at some point,” he tells Consequence on the eve of its upcoming Fathom Entertainment re-release. “That’s like your craziest, wildest dream, that people will be talking about your film 20 years later.” While the smirking, mustachioed mask is often associated with modern protests and resistance movements, the origins of the Guy Fawkes mask go even further back in history than writer Alan Moore and illustrator David Lloyd’s original comic series and graphic novel from the ’80s. The real-life Guy Fawkes was part of a group of Catholics who, feeling repressed by their anti-Catholic government, aimed to blow up the House of Lords (the famous “gunpowder plot”) on November 5th, 1606. Fawkes was captured and executed before he could complete his role in detonating the explosives, and November 5th became a national holiday in Britain, traditionally celebrated with bonfires. The idea of children dressing up as Fawkes first emerged in the late 18th century, evolving into variations on the iconic mask getting public distribution decades later. The definitive design of the Guy Fawkes mask, though, came from V for Vendetta artist Lloyd. The serialized comic book story that would eventually become the hit film began publishing in 1982, the mask’s history informing the choices of its central character. In the 2006 movie, the face of V, played by Hugo Weaving, is never seen — he only wears the famous mask. This created serious limitations for Weaving, since as McTeigue notes, “you don’t see the eyes. That’s the difference from Batman. It’s just this completely malleable face, and you can read into it what you want.” The movie’s design differed slightly from the graphic novel’s version, including some more textural detail in the goatee and eyebrows, and cheeks that were a little less ruddy. McTeigue describes his hope that it would work on screen as “blind faith,” considering that “it’s hard for an actor if you take away their face — you know, the thing that they’ve been working with for 30 or 40 years. But Hugo Weaving really got that it was about the physicality, and it was about the voice.” Additionally, McTeigue put a lot of work into exploring ways to make sure that the mask could take on different moods: “I did a bunch of lighting tests — lighting it in different ways so it could be benevolent, it could be vicious, it could be suspicious, all these different things. What does he look like lit from below, or from this side? What if one side’s completely dark? So by the time I got to film with it, depending on the overriding feeling I wanted in the scene, I could light the mask in the way I wanted. I would go, ‘Okay, let’s make him look sinister,’ so you’d light him from below. And when Evie comes out and tells the story of her parents, he’s very flatly lit, so he looks like he’s your grandfather you could have a nice chat to.” To enable that, there were variations of the mask that featured different finishes — some were highly glossed, and some were more matte in texture. “The gloss makes him feel like he’s very close to you, and the matte makes you feel like he’s a little ways away from you, and the light is sucking into it a little more,” explains McTeigue. “The way his hair fell sometimes, too, I’d mess with that as well.” The result is a movie that still feels shockingly relevant today, with broader ramifications for the rest of the world. Plenty of people had read the graphic novel, but McTeigue credits the influence of film as a medium on spreading awareness of the mask: “That film was number one at the box office, in America and overseas, when it came out. It was now exposed to millions and millions of people. And I think more importantly, people got what the mask was about, which was that there’s more power in ‘we’ than there is in ‘I.'” Additionally, protestors realized that the mask allowed them to remain anonymous, increasingly important as facial recognition software became widespread in the 21st century. “The Arab Spring got it, Occupy Wall Street got it, the Hong Kong protestors got it. Even the people protesting Scientology, which was the first time I saw it used as a form of protest, they got it,” McTeigue says, “and that made the mask live on and made the film live on as well. And so, yeah, now it’s completely seeped into the cultural vernacular.” The mild irony of this, especially for hacktivist protest groups like Anonymous, is that the mask’s origins in a comic series that eventually became a DC Comics property means that the design is owned by a corporation: Specifically, Warner Bros. gets a cut of every Lloyd-designed Guy Fawkes mask sold, and as of October 2026, David Ellison’s Skydance empire is the current owner of that copyright. V for Vendetta (Warner Bros., courtesy of Fathom Entertainment) This doesn’t diminish its power as a form of protest, or the movie’s legacy as an early example of how powerful comic book adaptations can be. “You have to remember, this is before the superhero saturation that we have now,” McTeigue says. “This is pre-the first Iron Man. Batman Begins had come out, but before that, it was the Tim Burton Batmans and the Supermans, which were very pop.” As a result, her says, “V for Vendetta was really before its time in a lot of ways, because it was an anti-superhero movie. Here’s this guy on this vengeful tear against the state, and all the people who had done him wrong, and the film is asking, at its core, ‘What’s the morality of terrorism?’ It’s a lofty thing to make a film about. You’re also trying to make it accessible, so there’s, the action set pieces and gunfights and blowing stuff up — all the things that might be popcorn entertainment. But there’s lots of other ideas underneath the surface of it.” And those ideas live on today — no small thanks to that mask. V for Vendetta returns to theaters for its 20th anniversary on November 1st and 5th, thanks to Fathom Entertainment. Visit the Fathom website for tickets and more information.

title: Two Years After World War II Ended, This Ship Brought the Bodies of 6,251 Fallen Service Members Back Home to America - Smithsonian Magazine
content:
Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine and get a FREE tote. The S.S. “Joseph V. Connolly” arrived in New York City on October 26, 1947. The caskets stored in its holds contained the remains of privates and three-star generals alike Robert Klara
        
        
          
            | History Correspondent The S.S. Joseph V. Connolly was one of 2,742 Liberty ships built during World War II. At 441.5 feet long and 57 feet wide at the beam, these cavernous vessels could haul 10,800 tons of whatever the United States Army required: ammunition, jeeps, tanks and even locomotives. Immense, rough-edged and clunky, the Liberty class wasn’t known for its looks. President Franklin D. Roosevelt even called the vessel “a real ugly duckling.” But on the morning of October 26, 1947, as it rolled in the swells just outside of New York Harbor, the Connolly was anything but ugly. Wreaths and garlands of laurel leaves draped the vessel’s bridge as its American flag snapped in the wind at half-mast. During the previous week at sea, the Connolly’s crew had slapped on a fresh coat of gray paint. As Captain Benjamin A. Bostelman guided his ship into port, U.S. Navy destroyers Beatty and Bristol swung into position ahead, their crews strewing flowers on the Connolly’s path. Meanwhile, a squadron of fighter planes joined the flotilla of police and fireboats in what the New York Times called a “marine escort of honor.” As the Connolly churned past Brooklyn and into Upper New York Bay, artillery pieces at Forts Hamilton, Wadsworth and Jay fired off 21-gun salutes. Never had a Liberty ship warranted a reception like this one—but technically speaking, the Connolly was no longer a Liberty ship. Following a reconfiguration of its holds earlier that year, the vessel had joined the Army’s newly created mortuary fleet, tasked with transporting the bodies of the fallen. On this unseasonably warm Sunday morning, the Connolly carried the remains of 6,251 war dead from the European theater. (The total number of coffins on board was 6,248; one of the caskets held the bodies of four men killed in an airplane crash in Newfoundland.) The Connolly’s arrival in New York, 79 years ago on Monday, was more than a day of mourning. It manifested one of the most solemn and arduous tasks that the U.S. government had ever attempted: the repatriation of the remains of every deceased World War II service member whose next of kin requested it. More than 400,000 American troops died during the conflict. The Army ultimately located the remains of 280,000 of them. Of that number, 171,752 would be returned to the U.S. “The Return of the World War II Dead Program was just an enormous effort,” says John C. McManus, a military historian at the Missouri University of Science and Technology and the author of more than a dozen books on the war. “It comes from the idea that the average person matters, that the state owes this to their next of kin, and to honor those who have died in the service of the country.” The Connolly’s journey was the culmination of a process that had begun long before, under circumstances the public could scarcely imagine. On May 16, 1946, Congress passed a law setting aside some $200 million for the “evacuation and return of the remains” of Americans who’d died in the war. In the weeks that followed, families of the fallen opened their mailboxes to find copies of “Tell Me About My Boy,” a pamphlet whose title was also the request most commonly received by the Army Quartermaster Corps, the office charged with locating, identifying and burying the dead. “While the war was on, most of these honored dead were buried in temporary United States military cemeteries,” the booklet read. Some of the fallen “were buried in isolated graves,” and these, the corps assured, “are being located as fast as possible.” But the pamphlet’s concise language barely hinted at the difficulty of this task. During the war, interment teams had followed the fighting, recording the locations of the soldiers they had buried in situ. As the pamphlet had alluded to, many of the fallen had been interred in temporary cemeteries—454 of them, to be exact, in 86 different countries on six continents. But thousands had been buried without being identified, and after the war ended in 1945, around 13,000 workers assigned to the Graves Registration Service began a worldwide sweep in search of them. In Europe alone, teams would scour 1.5 million square miles. Seeking to connect with anyone who might know the location of a buried infantryman, “jeep-riding propaganda teams” fanned out across France and Germany, the Quartermaster Corps noted in a report. They nailed up posters and placed notices in newspapers. In some cases, conscripted town criers walked through villages, hollering, “The American Army is searching for its dead!” Ultimately, the American Battle Monuments Commission established 15 military cemeteries for the soldiers slated to be interred near the theaters of battle. But the question of where exactly to bury these young service members began with the Quartermaster Corps’ second mailing to next-of-kin, which included a form titled “Request for Disposition of Remains.” Though the form presented the bereaved with four burial options, the choices for families really boiled down to just two. “The government is asking them, ‘Do you want your boy brought home?’” the Saturday Evening Post noted. “The families must soon say either, ‘Yes, bring him home,’ or, ‘Let him rest where he is.’” More than 60 percent of families decided that they wanted their loved ones returned to them. This, then, was the duty that the Connolly fulfilled as it steamed into New York Harbor on that October Sunday. Twenty-two days prior, the ship had cast off from Antwerp, Belgium, with “passengers deceased” (as the Army termed them) disinterred from the Henri-Chapelle American Cemetery near Liège. Cranes had lifted more caskets into the holds during a three-day stopover at Newfoundland’s Naval Station Argentia. The Connolly wasn’t the first vessel to take up this work. The Honda Knot had arrived in San Francisco on October 10, with 3,027 dead from the Pacific theater. But the Connolly carried double that number, and its arrival in New York—which had sent more troops into battle than any other port of embarkation in the U.S.—drew attention across the country. Aware of the spotlight about to be placed on the city, local officials planned a procession up Fifth Avenue for a single casket chosen from the Connolly’s holds. Honoring one unidentified soldier to mark the sacrifice of the many was a tradition dated to 1921, when the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier opened at Arlington National Cemetery. In this case, the identity of this soldier was known, although the Army never disclosed his name. The public learned that he was “a Congressional Medal of Honor man”—and that was all. “Ours is a species that deals with death, the concept, by dealing with our dead,” says poet, essayist and retired mortician Thomas Lynch. “So the wisdom of bringing our dead back home and assigning one of them—unknown to everybody there—was sufficient as an incarnation of the thing itself.” Saluting a single, emblematic soldier also provided a means of doing justice to the sheer number of the fallen, with their unique stories and their individual acts of heroism. The remains in the Connolly’s holds ranged from privates to three-star generals. They included Petty Officer Oscar A. Chaney, a Navy “flying sailor” who’d attempted to rescue a downed British air crew off the coast of Iceland, only to die of exposure after five days in a raft, as well as First Sergeant Americo Dorazio, who’d raced through a minefield to help an injured friend and lost his life doing it. “Without reservation,” his commanding officer had written to Dorazio’s mother, “your son was one of the finest soldiers I have ever had the privilege to command.” And then there was Second Lieutenant Frances Slanger, a nurse from Roxbury, Massachusetts, and the sole woman on the Connolly’s manifest. Insisting she be sent into action, Slanger had gone ashore in Normandy soon after D-Day, one of only four nurses to do so. In a field hospital near the Belgian front, Slanger had written an essay for Stars and Stripes about treating young men “brought in bloody, dirty with the earth, mud and grime,” some of them exclaiming at the sight of her: “Holy mackerel, an American woman!” Hours after Slanger dropped her story in the mail in October 1944, a shell fragment struck and killed her. Three years later, as New York City Mayor William O’Dwyer walked down the gangplank at Manhattan’s Pier 61, crew members had already positioned the casket on the Connolly’s deck. To the strains of Chopin’s funeral march, an honor guard of soldiers, sailors and marines bore the casket over the water, placing it on a horse-drawn auxiliary wagon for the procession. Still visible on Pier 61, painted over or fading, were the jubilant placards for the troops who’d returned home two years earlier: “Well Done” and “Welcome Home.” One of the Bristol’s ensigns turned to the sailor beside him and, reflecting on the Connolly’s passengers, said, “They came in too late.” A reconnaissance armored car eased the wagon east on 23rd Street before turning uptown at Fifth Avenue. Leading the procession was General Courtney Hodges, whose sentiments could only be imagined. As the International News Service observed, it was under Hodge’s command that “so many of these 6,200 died in the grueling march from Omaha Beach to the Elbe [River].” A company from the 325th Glider Infantry marched alongside the casket, forming the core of an honor guard numbering 6,000 and stretching for blocks. They included West Point cadets and midshipmen from the Naval Academy, a Marine company, and a Coast Guard platoon. Mounted police, Army nurses, war veterans and no fewer than eight bands also joined. Even the city’s Sanitation Department dispatched a contingent. On the sidewalks, packed crowds of onlookers in some places formed a solid mass. Estimates placed the number of spectators at 250,000, with another 150,000 filling Central Park for the memorial ceremony. The International News Service ballparked the total turnout at one million. “The curbs were crowded, but here, as at sea, the silence was awesome,” the New York Times wrote. “Nobody spoke, not even the children. Eyes were moist, and lips moved in prayer as the flag-draped coffin passed.” World War II had ended more than two years prior, yet the sight of the procession seemed to pull people back into it, opening wounds that had only just begun to heal. Onlookers watched the casket pass, “many of them weeping openly,” the Daily News reported. For many on the home front, the losses of the war had taken the form of telegrams and newspaper stories. But with the sight of a coffin, the war’s toll took on an immediacy that demanded attention. “Now it’s tangible—now you’re actually seeing it,” says John Curatola, a senior historian at the National WWII Museum in New Orleans. “For the first time, you see a mass casualty in terms of the actual sacrifice. That’s what’s so significant.” Emotions ran the highest during the ceremony in Central Park, where “elderly women and small boys and girls, joined by men in and out of uniform, gave way to their grief,” the Associated Press reported. As pallbearers moved the casket to a raised platform, a mother in the front row began to scream her son’s name. “Johnny!” she wailed. “There’s my boy. There’s my boy.” Officials took turns at the microphone, with New York Governor Thomas Dewey using his time on stage to warn of the growing threat posed by communism: “In Europe, in Asia, all over the world,” he said, “governments are under heavy attack from the agents of the totalitarian left. Their very existence is threatened.” In a fitting riposte from his pulpit, meanwhile, the Reverend Theodore Cuyler Speers suggested that “silence in the presence of the one anonymous coffin would be of greater value than many speeches.” At 8 a.m. on October 27, the Connolly slipped away from Manhattan and steamed south to its next, and logistically most important, stop. This was the Brooklyn Army Terminal, a concrete colossus that had packed off 37 million tons of military supplies and 3.2 million troops over the course of the war. The Connolly tied up at Pier 3, where a small memorial service got underway from a temporary stage below the trusses. “No matter what you may think about the way things are going today, this would not have been so had the other side won,” Brooklyn Borough President John Cashmore told some 2,500 mourners. But the time for commemoration was now over, ceding its place to the essential work at hand. As the crowds trickled away, the Connolly’s deck cranes began hoisting the caskets onto the pier, where a kind of industrial ballet of men and machines began. “You can think about it as all the logistics they’ve done for the war—in reverse,” says Andrew Gustafson, who regularly leads visitors around the Brooklyn complex as the vice president of Turnstile Tours. “These people coming back were the war dead, but they were treated just like they were living service members.” Workers first opened the wooden shipping containers enclosing each casket, checking for and repairing any damage before the Graves Registration Service sent notifications to next-of-kin. Battery-powered tractors then towed the containers over a skybridge to the atrium of a different building, where, 101 feet below the plate-glass roof, teams loaded them onto mortuary cars parked on a pair of railroad tracks. Once assembled, these trains departed the terminal, bound for one of 15 national distribution centers in cities like Atlanta, Fort Worth and Chicago. Gathered at those destinations were men in immaculate uniforms, with black mourning bands on their left upper sleeves. These were the personal escorts who would accompany the deceased to the final station stops, with one man assigned to each casket. The escorts were the U.S. Army’s finest, each exhibiting “the highest uniform standards, proper comportment, professionalism [and] military courtesy,” McManus says. “They’re literally the face of the United States government.” They would also, at times, be the faces that reminded the bereaved of the sons, brothers or husbands they had lost. In the months to come, letters would pour into the terminal from families who’d been consoled in their grief by the escorts. In at least one instance, parents offered to adopt one of the young men. Venturing into the complex the following year, a Brooklyn Eagle reporter observed the “deep sense of responsibility” the escorts felt for the remains entrusted to them. The author understood why: “His thoughts, particularly if he’s a combat veteran, run something like this: ‘… But for the grace of God, it might have been me.’” It would take days to unload the Connolly, and even then, when the ship’s holds were finally empty, the work had only just begun. “In the years to come,” the New York Herald Tribune observed, “nearly 100,000 dead soldiers, sailors and Marines still resting below white crosses in Europe will follow this first contingent home.” In the early hours of January 12, 1948, the ship caught fire 1,000 miles east of New York, en route to Antwerp. Nearby vessels rescued all 46 men on board—including Captain Bostelman—before the Connolly sank with 6,445 caskets still in its holds. Fortunately, all of them were empty. Robert Klara

title: Mate Rimac Hints At Stick Shift, Non-Hybrid Bugatti Based On the V-16 Tourbillion - Road & Track
content: Yes, that would mean a manual transmission hooked up directly to a V-16 engine. While he initially split ownership of Bugatti with Porsche, electric supercar pioneer Mate Rimac is now in full control of the hypercar manufacturer. That opens the door for all kinds of wild ideas—and Rimac is not exactly subtle about his interest in them. In an interview with Top Gear published on Sunday, he indicated that one of those ideas is a manual, hybrid-free V-16 car based on the Tourbillion. Rimac suggests that the car would be a return to historic form for Bugatti, noting that “the Tourbillon as it is now made a lot of sense as a successor to the Chiron. It’s an incredible car... But I wonder myself, what’s next for Bugatti and what would be interesting to do? And I think light weight and simplification of stuff... Instead of a sledgehammer as Bugattis were the last 20 years, could you do something that’s also more engaging, more back to the roots, more Type 35?” The suggestion comes months after Rimac first told Road & Track about his interest in a manual V-16 model based on the Tourbillon back in August. He suggested a “real manual” back then, indicating that it would be a conventional gearbox in direct control rather than a simulated system like that used in the Ferrari 12Cilindri Manuale. That’s exciting enough on its own, but the idea of lightening the car, potentially by removing the entire hybrid powertrain, is a new wrinkle. While the hybrid Tourbillon boasts 1800 horsepower in total, 973 of that comes from the internal combustion engine. Add in the weight potentially dropped by removing batteries and electric motors, and you’d have the recipe for a relatively light, relatively simple hypercar that still boasts nearly 1000 hp from a naturally-aspirated V-16 engine. That sounds thrilling, to say the least. If Bugatti ever does build such a car, it should have no issue selling out ... at whatever price Rimac and his company choose. Fred Smith's love of cars comes from his fascination with auto racing. Unfortunately, that passion led him to daily drive a high-mileage, first-year Porsche Panamera. title: Roth v. Trump - | Knight First Amendment Institute
content: A lawsuit challenging President Trump’s policy of expelling reporters from the White House. On October 26, 2026, the Knight Institute and the Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School filed a lawsuit challenging President Trump’s policy of expelling journalists and news organizations from the White House for reporting that he characterizes as “fake news.” Filed on behalf of a human rights advocate, a media watchdog, a historian, a civics teacher, a legal journalist, and a student journalist, the lawsuit contends that the president’s effort to destroy the White House press corps’ independence is an unconstitutional attack on the public’s right to trustworthy and undistorted reporting about the president and his policies. The lawsuit argues that the spaces that the White House has opened up to the White House Press Corps for newsgathering and related activities are a “public forum” under the First Amendment and that the government can’t constitutionally exclude news organizations from these spaces on the basis of viewpoint. title: Measure V parcel tax costs ‘less than a Netflix subscription,’ WCCUSD says. Here's what it pays for - Richmondside
content: Independent nonprofit news for Richmond, CA A parcel tax that funds libraries, sports and staffing at West Contra Costa schools is up for renewal this November, and many students and staff fear what they might lose if it fails. Measure V, which generates about $10 million annually, has been a critical source of funding for WCCUSD. Since 2004, it has been renewed every four to eight years to raise money for sports and school libraries and to hire dozens of staff, from counselors and speech therapists to custodians and school safety officers. The rate has remained the same since 2004 — 7.2 cents per square foot of total building area — costing an average homeowner about $96 per year, according to WCCUSD. Seniors and disabled property owners are exempt. “It’s less than a Netflix subscription,” WCCUSD spokesperson Liz Sanders told Richmondside. The school board voted to keep the rate the same to help increase the likelihood of its passage. Such measures aren’t guaranteed to win given they require two-thirds voter approval. In the June primary election, the Contra Costa Community College’s Measure G failed. The bond would have raised money to improve campus infrastructures. If Measure V fails, the district says it will either need to find an additional $8 million a year or find things to cut. Richmondside looked more closely at how the money was spent from 2015 to 2025 to help voters understand where their dollars are going. On average, the bulk of the money funds school libraries, about $3.5 million each year. The next highest categories were $1.5 million to fund afterschool sports programs and $1.3 million on hiring staff including counselors, psychologists and special education aides. WCCUSD spent an average of $950,000 a year on core academics, including supplementing teacher salaries and buying textbooks or other curriculum. It spent the least on school safety, spending about $350,000 a year to hire custodians or school safety officers and the supplies they need. The spending amounts vary, but the five priority areas remained the same. WCCUSD also allocates some portion of the dollars to charter schools, an amount that has been gradually increased annually to about $2 million currently, as the number of students going to charter schools has increased. How the money is spent in upcoming years, assuming it passes, is unlikely to change much because for more than 25 years, voters have been relatively consistent with their preferences. “There are some additional (funding) areas that are named … and that comes from the polling that we do,” Sanders said. “For example, attracting and receiving high-quality teachers and STEAM (science, technology, engineering, the arts, and mathematics) education.” A board-commissioned survey by Godbe Research found that if the measure went before voters today, about 65.8% of voters would say yes — about 1% less than the two-thirds majority needed. The same survey also found that the community wants to see more investment in the arts, so the ballot language was changed to indicate that. It also was adjusted to include an emphasis on preparing students “for the changing economy.” “We’re trying to keep the language in the ballot measure updated enough that it will be able to fund local priorities through the term of the measure (which is nine years),” Sanders said. “We want to make sure that in five years, seven years, eight years, the language in the tax will still be relevant to the things that we might want to be funding, or that the community priorities might apply.” How a measure is written is critical because it defines where exactly dollars are allowed to be spent. Including the word “art” for example, means the district can then allocate funding for such programs, especially if and when grant funding for a current arts program comes to an end. The current measure specifically says dollars will be used for “protecting core academics, science, music, arts and career technical programs that prepare students for the changing economy; attracting and retaining qualified teachers; and maintaining mental health services and counselors to support student success.” In the last 10 years, the parcel tax has been used to fund at least 30 full-time librarian salaries districtwide — until 2024. In 2015, WCCUSD had the equivalent of almost 40 full-time equivalent employees in specialties including elementary school librarians and media specialists. In 2025, there were 22 full-time equivalent employees. The number decreased over the decade as educator salaries increased and the district’s budget tightened. Last year, the school district cut library budgets even further, leaving elementary schools without a full-time librarian this year. Tracy LaFreniere, a first grade teacher at Ellerhorst Elementary in Pinole, said her students now go to the library once every two weeks and can’t visit it at other times. She worries what the future could look like if Measure V isn’t renewed. Helms Middle School librarian Jon Henry Evans said if Measure V doesn’t pass, his job is at risk. “The measure funds us being here. If the measure is not renewed this school may no longer have a position for me, which would be really devastating for me, to be honest,” Evans told Richmondside. “But in addition to that, it also funds (buying) most of our books.” A librarian can play a critical role in a school, not only in helping improve literacy but also in creating a culture of intellectual curiosity and community. In Evan’s library, he applies for grants and secures various funding to buy things like bean bag chairs, a button maker, board games and a “take care station” that provides students with toiletries such as toothbrushes or hair combs. He has also created a “library of things,” where students can check out items including a ukulele, a stop motion animation kit or a bird watching kit. “They’re able to use these tools or these resources to explore hobbies or interests in ways that they might not be able to otherwise,” Evans told Richmondside. “We’re about supporting information exchange. We’re about supporting our community, but we don’t just do that through books anymore.” He said the library this year is the busiest it has ever been, filled with students every lunch period. Evans has been at Helms for 12 years. He initially taught English language development for six years but decided to get his library credential and switched roles in 2021. “I realized the best thing I could do for my students was to get them to be readers,” Evans said. “All of these standards that we teach, all the content that we teach, it all matters. It’s all important. But reading gives the student the ability to learn these things for themselves … that’s kind of the number one thing that you can do to set a student up for future success.” As a librarian, he said he tries to improve student reading by making sure they provide the books kids want to read. He also provides training for teachers and helps match books to a student’s particular interests to foster a love of reading. “There’s a lot of things that we do all day,” Evans said. “For some of our elementary school teachers who split their time between sites, I don’t really know how they do it.” “I don’t think I could maintain my collection or all of my programs if I weren’t here all day every day,” he continued. “But even with that, the funding that it takes to keep a library up and running is (not enough). We oftentimes find ourselves looking for alternate funding sources like donors. Many of us apply for grants. None of that happens if there’s not a school librarian to seek those funding opportunities.” Every year the district allocates about $1.5 million of the funding for afterschool sports. The dollars are evenly distributed among school sites, which then determine how to use them. It is among several sources of funding for afterschool programming. About half of the funding pays for coaches, and the other half is for gear, equipment and other needs. However, even with dedicated funding, it’s still only just enough to provide the bare minimum for some sports, students and staff told Richmondside. At De Anza High School, the cross country team, for example, appears to be hanging on by a thread. For weeks leading up to the season, the team did not have a coach. Students wear old mismatched jerseys, and parents subsidize costs for snacks, water and other race day necessities. Fou Mikaio, the school’s athletic director, stepped up to coach the team herself because she couldn’t find anyone to fill the role. She said because the pay is low, it’s hard to recruit high quality coaches to train the students. “For varsity, the pay is about $21,000 (for the part-time coaching job),” Mikaio told Richmondside at an October cross country meet. “The pay has been the same forever.” If Measure V isn’t renewed, she worries coaching pay will be cut or remain stagnant, making it even harder to hire coaches for all sports. It could also be more difficult to replace aging equipment, she said. De Anza senior Daniel Akagi, a varsity cross country runner, said he canvassed for the measure, even though he’s graduating, because of how transformational it has been for him. “I wasn’t really an active person my freshman year,” Akagi told Richmondside before a 2-mile race. “But when I started (in sophomore year), it made me be a more outgoing person, I got more fit, and also you get to meet new people from your team itself … I felt like I started to just explore the world.” He said it worries him that underclassmen may not have the same opportunities,speculating that a sport like cross country could be the first to get cut when hard decisions need to be made. He said without the renewal, it could also lead to other cuts at the school. Last year, the WCCUSD board voted to cut De Anza’s class schedule from seven to six classes a semester to balance a budget deficit. For students, that means fewer elective options and fewer Advanced Placement (AP) classes offered. Senior Claire LaFreniere said the arts were impacted the most. Ceramics and AP art were cut from the schedule. “Our teachers also just don’t have supplies,” said LaFreniere, who has been taking art classes all of high school. “With my art teacher, all the stuff that he has in his classroom, he buys himself, and it’s like all of it, like the paint, the brushes … I don’t think we’ve had new supplies in a while.” The school’s band program was also at risk of being cut, but was saved at the eleventh-hour. However, it’s now an afterschool program, instead of an elective class. “They have to practice outside of school because they don’t have room for their elective (with the schedule change),” LaFreniere said. She said her brother’s friend who wanted to run cross country again this year, couldn’t because band practice was at the same time. Akagi said he really hopes the community votes to renew the parcel tax. He was inspired to canvas through his work with the Richmond Fire Youth Academy (Richmond voters are also considering a sales tax to help fix the city’s fire stations.)  After graduation, he plans to go to Contra Costa Community College and become a firefighter. “If (you want kids) to plan to go to college, they should have better access to better honors classes, AP classes; have better sports equipment; things like that,” Akagi said. “These things help (students) be better, and make their college applications better.” Editor’s note: Story was updated to reflect the average cost of the parcel tax of per-household based on the district’s calculations. title: When Holding a Person’s ID for a Warrant Check Becomes a Seizure: Commonwealth v. Bennett - Serpa Law Office
content: By Attorney Joe Serpa | Georgetown University Law Center On October 19, 2026, the Massachusetts Appeals Court held in Commonwealth v. Bennett, No. 25-P-1445, that a police officer seized a man when the officer took the man’s identification card and held it while calling in a warrant check. Because the officer did not have reasonable suspicion that the man had committed a crime when the seizure occurred, the court held that the seizure was unlawful and affirmed the suppression of the suspected fentanyl the police found afterward. Bennett is an unpublished summary decision under Appeals Court Rule 23.0, so a court may cite it for its persuasive value but not as binding precedent. The decision still shows how a routine street encounter becomes a seizure under settled Supreme Judicial Court law. The police approached the defendant and asked whether he needed assistance or medical attention. The Appeals Court agreed with the parties and the motion judge that the officers were acting within their community caretaking function when they first approached and spoke with him. The officer then took the defendant’s identification card and held it while requesting a warrant check. The warrant check revealed a warrant, the police arrested the defendant, and a search of his backpack produced the suspected fentanyl. The defendant moved to suppress the fentanyl, and a District Court judge allowed the motion. The Commonwealth appealed, and the Appeals Court affirmed the order suppressing the evidence. A person is seized by the police when an officer, through words or conduct, communicates that the officer will use police authority to require the person to stay. Commonwealth v. Matta, 483 Mass. 357 (2019). The Appeals Court held that the officer communicated exactly that when the officer took the defendant’s identification card and held it while running the warrant check, because a reasonable person would understand that he had to stay at least until the dispatcher answered. The court relied on Commonwealth v. Lyles, 453 Mass. 811 (2009), in which the Supreme Judicial Court held that an officer seized a person by requesting and taking the person’s identification and calling in a warrant check. The court held that the calm tone and the brief length of the encounter did not change the result. The defendant was seized the moment the officer took the identification card and called in the warrant check. A seizure requires that the police have reasonable suspicion that the person has committed, is committing, or is about to commit a crime. Commonwealth v. Palmer, 498 Mass. 117 (2026). The court held that the police did not have reasonable suspicion of any crime at the moment of the seizure, so the seizure was unlawful. The police may approach a person and offer assistance as part of their community caretaking function without seizing the person. A community caretaking encounter becomes a seizure, however, when the officer’s words or conduct communicate that the person must stay. The Appeals Court held that the encounter became a seizure when the officer took and held the identification card to run the warrant check, and that the community caretaking function did not justify that seizure. The Commonwealth argued that the warrant check furthered officer safety. The Appeals Court rejected that argument on this record because the Commonwealth presented no evidence that this defendant posed a specific danger to the officers. The court noted that the Supreme Judicial Court has refused to adopt a blanket rule allowing a patfrisk before transporting a person as community caretaking, and has required a reasonable basis for that more limited step. Because a warrant check is less connected to officer safety than a patfrisk, the Commonwealth needed at least the same justification for the warrant check, and the Commonwealth offered no evidence of one. A person who hands an officer identification during a street encounter may already be seized once the officer keeps the identification and runs a warrant check. Where the police lack reasonable suspicion of a crime at that moment, a court can suppress the evidence the police find after the warrant check, including evidence found during a search that followed an arrest on a warrant the check revealed. The analysis depends on when the seizure occurred and what the police knew at that moment. A defendant who wants to suppress evidence from this kind of encounter should establish, through the police reports and the officers’ testimony, the exact point at which the officer took the identification and called in the warrant check, and what facts the officer knew at that point. Because Bennett is a Rule 23.0 summary decision, counsel should cite the Supreme Judicial Court decisions it applies, Matta, Lyles, and Palmer, as the binding authority, and cite Bennett only as a persuasive application of those decisions.
